captions: Let's break down the Shiprocket I-P-O —
a one thousand six hundred and seventeen crore issue from a well-known e-commerce logistics platform.
There's one thing that makes valuing this company different from the others this week —
it doesn't yet make a profit.
We'll cover the business, the financials, the money trail,
how it compares to rivals, and how to apply.
This is education, not investment advice.
So what does Shiprocket do?
It's a software platform that helps online sellers ship their orders.
From one dashboard,
a seller can pick from more than seventeen courier partners —
but Shiprocket itself owns no trucks or warehouses.
It's asset-light.
Around that, it offers a full toolkit — checkout, returns,
packaging, even financing —
for small online sellers and D2C brands.
So it's a picks-and-shovels play on India's e-commerce boom: it grows as the number of small online sellers grows,
rather than betting on any single store.
Let's go deeper.
Who's actually on the platform?
In FY twenty twenty-six,
Shiprocket served about two point one five lakh active merchants —
mostly small and D-2-C sellers —
reaching over a hundred and fifty-five million end consumers across nineteen thousand-plus pin codes.
As a platform there's no order book; the scale metric is volume —
it processes more than twenty-five million shipments a month and around two hundred million transactions a year.
Small and solo sellers are about sixty percent of the base,
while venture-backed D-2-C brands in beauty,
fashion and electronics are its fastest-growing revenue.
Now the financials, and this is the key part.
Revenue for FY twenty twenty-six was about two thousand and twenty-four crore,
up twenty-four percent.
But the company is still loss-making —
it lost about seventy-nine crore.
The good news is how sharply that loss has shrunk: from a huge five hundred and ninety-five crore loss two years ago,
to seventy-nine crore now.
So the trend is strongly in the right direction —
but remember, it does not yet make a profit,
and that changes how you value it.
Where does your money go?
Of the one thousand six hundred and seventeen crore issue,
about eight hundred and eighty-six crore —
some fifty-five percent —
is a fresh issue that goes into the company.
The remaining seven hundred and thirty-two crore is an Offer for Sale,
where early investors sell part of their stake.
So it's a fairly balanced split —
a little over half is fresh money for the business,
and the rest lets early backers take some money off the table.
What does the fresh money fund?
The main use is marketing and technology,
across both its core shipping business and newer lines —
the fuel it needs to keep growing and, hopefully,
reach profit.
Part is set aside for potential acquisitions and to repay some borrowings.
And the rest is general corporate purposes.
So the money is aimed squarely at growth —
which is what a company still chasing profitability needs.
Now the competitors — and here the maths is different,
because Shiprocket loses money, so there's no P-E to quote.
Its main listed benchmark is Delhivery,
India's largest logistics company,
worth over twenty-five thousand crore.
But Delhivery OWNS the trucks,
hubs and warehouses; Shiprocket is asset-light —
it just aggregates seventeen courier partners under one dashboard.
It also competes with the listed enabler Unicommerce,
and unlisted names like Xpressbees and Shadowfax —
a crowded field.
Because it's loss-making,
investors value it on price-to-SALES —
roughly three and a half times revenue at its seven-thousand-crore price —
and on how fast those losses are shrinking,
from nearly six hundred crore down to under eighty.
Should you subscribe?
The strengths — revenue up twenty-four percent,
losses cut by nearly ninety percent in two years,
and an asset-light,
scalable model that rides the whole D2C wave.
The watch-outs — it's still loss-making,
so there's no P-E; the market is crowded and competitive; and about forty-five percent is a sell-down,
with the company valued on sales rather than profit.
The takeaway — a fast-improving,
asset-light platform with a real path to profit,
but not there yet.
Judge it as a growth bet, not a value one.
How do you apply, and how much do you need?
Retail investors bid up to two lakh for a thirty-five percent quota,
with allotment by lottery if oversubscribed.
H-N-Is go above two lakh for a fifteen percent quota.
For Shiprocket, one lot is a hundred and fifty-four shares —
about fourteen thousand nine hundred and thirty-eight rupees —
your minimum.
Track the live subscription on the N-S-E and B-S-E I-P-O pages,
Chittorgarh, Moneycontrol, or your broker app.
Let's recap Shiprocket.
An asset-light e-commerce shipping platform —
a picks-and-shovels play on D2C,
with revenue up twenty-four percent and losses cut sharply.
The issue is about fifty-five percent fresh,
the rest a sell-down.
The key point — it's still loss-making,
so there's no P-E; it's valued on sales,
near three and a half times revenue,
and against listed Delhivery.
The retail minimum is about fourteen thousand nine hundred and thirty-eight rupees,
and the grey-market premium is near fourteen percent,
though unofficial.
This video explains the IPO for education only —
it is not investment advice,
not a buy or sell recommendation,
and not a prediction of listing gains.
Grey-market premium is unofficial and changes hourly.
Always read the RHP and check the live subscription before you apply.
Thanks for watching.
